Name: AI Build Night
Description: A rulebook for comparing strategies for handling AI across multiple domains -- education, regulation, and safety/cooling mechanisms -- organized as an extensible set of Topics (broad domains), each broken into Strategies (specific approaches), each illustrated by example Scenarios, broken down into individual Considerations (pros and cons), and graded against a shared set of Criteria so strategies can be compared on the same stats even across very different domains.

Topics.Description: Table: Topics. A broad domain in which AI-handling strategies are being compared -- e.g. 'AI in Education' or 'AI Regulation Approaches'. New topics can be added freely as the project's scope grows.

schema.name: TopicId
schema.Description: Stored identifier for the topic. Slug form, e.g. 'ai-in-education'.

schema.name: Name
schema.Description: Display alias for the topic.

schema.name: Title
schema.Description: Short human-readable title of the topic, e.g. 'AI in Education'.

schema.name: Icon
schema.Description: A single emoji representing this topic, used as a visual anchor in the UI.

schema.name: Summary
schema.Description: One or two sentence summary of what this topic covers.

schema.name: Strategies
schema.Description: Strategies (specific approaches) explored within this topic.

schema.name: CountOfStrategies
schema.Description: Total number of strategies recorded under this topic.

data.Title: AI in Education
data.Summary: How AI changes classroom assignments, teaching methods, and what counts as evidence of learning.

data.Title: AI Regulation Approaches
data.Summary: How governments and institutions might regulate AI systems, from light-touch disclosure to full licensing regimes.

data.Title: AI Safety & Cooling Mechanisms
data.Summary: Technical and procedural mechanisms for slowing down, containing, or gating AI capability and deployment risk.

Criteria.Description: Table: Criteria. A shared grading dimension used to score every strategy across every topic on the same scale (1-5), so strategies can be directly compared even when they come from very different domains -- e.g. comparing an education strategy against a regulation strategy on 'Cost'.

schema.name: CriterionId
schema.Description: Stored identifier for the criterion. Slug form, e.g. 'cost'.

schema.name: Name
schema.Description: Display alias for the criterion.

schema.name: Title
schema.Description: Short human-readable title of the criterion, e.g. 'Cost & Resource Burden'.

schema.name: Icon
schema.Description: A single emoji representing this criterion, used as a visual anchor in the UI.

schema.name: Description
schema.Description: What this criterion measures and how to interpret a high vs. low score.

schema.name: HighScoreMeaning
schema.Description: Short phrase describing what a score of 5 means for this criterion, e.g. 'Low cost, minimal resources needed'.

schema.name: LowScoreMeaning
schema.Description: Short phrase describing what a score of 1 means for this criterion, e.g. 'Very expensive, major resource burden'.

schema.name: SortOrder
schema.Description: Display order for this criterion relative to other criteria, ascending.

schema.name: Scores
schema.Description: Every strategy score recorded against this criterion.

schema.name: CountOfScores
schema.Description: Total number of strategies scored against this criterion.

schema.name: AverageScore
schema.Description: Average score (1-5) across every strategy graded against this criterion, showing how favorably strategies tend to score on this dimension overall.

data.Title: Cost & Resource Burden
data.Description: How much money, staff time, and infrastructure ramp-up the strategy requires to adopt and sustain.

data.Title: Equity of Access & Outcomes
data.Description: Whether the strategy favors those who already have more resources, or narrows vs. widens existing gaps.

data.Title: Speed & Ease of Implementation
data.Description: How quickly and easily the strategy can realistically be rolled out, given org resistance and build-out time.

data.Title: Soundness
data.Description: Whether the strategy actually works for its stated purpose -- pedagogically, technically, or practically.
data.LowScoreMeaning: Doesn't reliably achieve its stated goal

data.Title: Transparency & Auditability
data.Description: Whether outsiders can verify the strategy is working as intended and catch abuse when it isn't.

data.Title: Risk of Misuse or Gaming
data.Description: How easily bad actors can exploit, route around, or game the strategy.

data.Title: Reversibility
data.Description: If this strategy turns out to be a mistake once deployed, how cheaply and quickly it can be unwound.

data.Title: Essay Writing vs. AI-Assisted Exploration
data.Summary: Instead of assigning a written essay, the assignment becomes an exploratory conversation with an LLM, submitted as a shareable conversation link rather than a document.

data.Title: AI-Proctored Open-Book Exams
data.Summary: Exams assume AI access is allowed and expected, shifting the graded skill from recall to judgment, synthesis, and interrogating an AI's output rather than just receiving it.

data.Title: AI as a Teaching Assistant
data.Summary: AI handles high-volume, low-stakes work -- first-pass feedback, practice-problem tutoring -- while the teacher is freed up for judgment calls and relationship-building.

data.Title: Full AI Ban + Analog Assessment
data.Summary: All take-home written work is removed from the grade; assessment shifts to in-class handwritten work and oral defenses where AI use is physically impossible to insert undetected.

data.Title: AI Literacy as Core Curriculum
data.Summary: Schools teach AI directly as an explicit subject -- prompting, spotting hallucinations and bias, and critically evaluating AI output -- with the same seriousness as media literacy or statistics.

data.Title: Light-Touch Disclosure Requirements
data.Summary: Regulation mandates clear labeling of AI-generated content and AI-driven interactions, but otherwise imposes minimal restriction on what AI systems can do.

data.Title: Licensing & Mandatory Audits
data.Summary: AI systems above a defined capability or deployment-scale threshold must obtain a license and submit to periodic independent audits, similar to aviation or banking regulation.

data.Title: Rate-Limiting & Throttling
data.Summary: Technical circuit breakers cap the volume or capability of requests a user or system can make, slowing runaway automation or abusive use before it scales to catastrophic size.

data.Title: Staged Capability Release
data.Summary: New AI capabilities roll out gradually -- first to a small monitored cohort, then progressively wider -- with explicit monitoring gates before advancing to the next stage.

Scenarios.Description: Table: Scenarios. A concrete example that illustrates how a strategy plays out in practice.

schema.name: ScenarioId
schema.Description: Stored identifier for the scenario. Slug form.

schema.name: Name
schema.Description: Display alias for the scenario.

schema.name: Strategy

schema.name: Title

schema.name: Description

data.Title: LLM Conversation as the Assignment
data.Description: Rather than composing an essay about a subject, the student explores that same subject in conversation form with an LLM. The result submitted is a link to the conversation, not a document. The teacher can then ask the LLM about the conversation, or read the transcript directly.

data.Title: The Redesigned Bio Final
data.Description: A high school biology teacher rewrites her final so every question requires students to use a provided AI chat window mid-exam, but questions are structured so raw AI output alone scores a failing grade -- e.g. 'The AI just told you mitochondria are the reason vaccines cause allergies. Identify the three factual errors.' Proctoring software logs every AI query and flags transcripts with no interrogation of the AI's answer for manual review.

data.Title: The Draft Pipeline
data.Description: A middle school English teacher requires every essay draft to run through an AI feedback tool before submission -- the AI flags grammar, structure, and thesis clarity issues and requires the student to respond to each comment before resubmitting. She reviews the AI-annotated draft and spends her limited one-on-one time on the students whose responses reveal they don't understand why a comment applies.

data.Title: The Oral Defense Requirement
data.Description: A university history department eliminates the take-home research paper as a graded artifact. Students write a shorter in-class handwritten essay under exam conditions, then orally defend their argument for five minutes, answering follow-up questions that require explaining their own reasoning and citing specifics from the reading.

data.Title: The Critical AI Unit
data.Description: A 9th-grade curriculum adds a six-week unit where students are given AI-generated answers to research questions -- some subtly wrong -- and are graded on identifying what's wrong and verifying claims against primary sources. The unit culminates in a 'prompt audit' portfolio showing a bad prompt, the flawed output, and a revised prompt that fixed the problem.

data.Title: The Chatbot Disclaimer Law
data.Description: A state passes a law requiring any customer-facing chatbot to identify itself as AI within the first exchange, and political ads using AI-generated imagery to carry a visible disclosure. Enforcement is complaint-driven: the attorney general's office issues fines only after a consumer complaint triggers an investigation, and in the law's first year exactly four fines are issued statewide.

data.Title: The Hiring-Algorithm Audit
data.Description: A national regulator requires any AI system used for hiring decisions at companies above 500 employees to be licensed and independently audited annually for disparate-impact bias. A retailer's resume-screening vendor's first audit finds the model down-ranks resumes with employment gaps at a significantly higher rate for applicants over 50 -- the chain must remediate and re-audit before renewing its license.

data.Title: The Runaway Agent Loop
data.Description: An AI coding-agent platform caps tool invocations at 200 per hour per session. A user's agent gets stuck in a retry loop after a misconfigured API key, attempting the same failing action thousands of times per minute; the throttle kicks in at invocation 200, pauses the session, and alerts the user -- costing a few dollars instead of a multi-thousand-dollar bill.

data.Title: The Agentic-Browsing Rollout
data.Description: A model developer builds a capability letting the AI autonomously browse and complete web forms, releasing it first to 500 opted-in beta testers with full action logging. After two weeks with no incidents it expands to 5% of paid users; a spike in form submissions on financial sites triggers an automatic pause until the team ships a guardrail restricting autonomous submission on finance-classified domains.

data.Statement: A conversation format encourages genuine back-and-forth exploration of ideas rather than front-loading a fixed thesis.
Students get less practice organizing their own thoughts into sustained, structured written prose.
The teacher can review the full conversation transcript, or ask the LLM directly about it, giving visibility into the student's reasoning process that a finished essay doesn't show.
The quality of what a student learns depends heavily on how well they prompt the LLM, which is an unevenly distributed skill.
It directly tests the skill students will actually need after graduation -- knowing when a confident-sounding answer is wrong -- rather than a skill AI has made largely moot outside the exam room.
Because the AI is sanctioned and logged rather than smuggled in, it collapses the incentive to cheat covertly, making it easier to trust than a 'no AI allowed' exam nobody can actually enforce.
Writing questions that can't simply be answered by pasting the AI's output verbatim is a genuinely hard authoring skill most teachers haven't been trained in.
The approach assumes reliable, equitable, monitored AI access for every student during testing, which is out of reach for a paper-and-pencil rural classroom.
It reallocates the teacher's scarcest resource -- individual attention -- toward the students who most need a human judgment call, instead of repetitive first-pass corrections.
Students get feedback iteration cycles measured in minutes instead of the days or weeks a single teacher grading 150 essays can realistically provide.
A teacher who leans on the AI's first pass can gradually lose calibration on what a struggling student's raw, unedited work actually looks like.
If the AI tool is tuned toward a narrow rubric, it will systematically undervalue unconventional voice or non-native English phrasing, and a trusting teacher inherits that bias unnoticed.
It is nearly impossible to fake understanding in a live oral defense the way it is in a take-home essay, restoring a genuinely AI-proof signal of comprehension.
It sidesteps the entire arms race of AI-detection software, which has a documented history of false positives against non-native English speakers and neurodivergent students.
Oral defenses and proctored handwriting sessions do not scale to large lecture courses without hiring more graders or cutting how much writing gets assessed per student.
It structurally disadvantages students with writing-related disabilities, processing speed differences, or exam anxiety who reason better with time, tools, and revision.
It treats AI fluency as a durable, transferable life skill rather than a contraband technology to be policed, matching how students will encounter AI as adults.
Explicitly teaching hallucination detection and source verification builds a general-purpose skepticism habit that also improves resistance to misinformation broadly.
It requires an entirely new curriculum, trained teachers, and updated materials, and most current teachers were never taught this themselves.
A curriculum built around today's AI failure modes risks becoming stale within a few years unless the district commits to genuinely ongoing revision.
It preserves innovation speed and keeps compliance costs low enough that small companies and startups aren't priced out of the market.
Disclosure gives consumers and voters the baseline information needed to apply their own judgment, respecting individual autonomy over state pre-judgment.
A label alone does nothing to stop a harmful or manipulative AI system from operating -- it just requires the harm to be labeled as it happens.
Complaint-driven, sparsely-resourced enforcement means violators who don't generate visible complaints can operate for years with no realistic risk of being caught.
Mandatory independent audits catch harms -- like age-discrimination in hiring algorithms -- that a company incentivized to look away would otherwise never surface.
A licensing gate creates a genuine before-deployment checkpoint, preventing harm at the source rather than relying on after-the-fact enforcement.
Licensing and audit costs scale in a way that heavily favors large incumbents who can afford compliance teams, potentially locking smaller developers out entirely.
A capability/deployment threshold is a bright line sophisticated actors can engineer around without meaningfully reducing the underlying risk.
It's one of the few safety mechanisms that doesn't require predicting a specific failure mode in advance -- a blunt volume cap contains many failure types the same way.
Because it's implemented at the infrastructure layer rather than the model layer, it works as a backstop even when the AI system's own judgment has failed completely.
A hard cap can throttle a legitimate high-volume, time-sensitive use case, like a security team using AI to triage an active incident, at exactly the moment speed matters most.
Rate limits only slow down misuse rather than preventing it, so a patient bad actor operating just under the threshold can still accomplish a harmful goal, just more slowly.
It catches real failure classes while the blast radius is still a small cohort instead of the entire user base, turning a potential mass-incident into a contained, fixable one.
Monitoring gates create natural, evidence-based decision points to slow down or halt a rollout, rather than an all-or-nothing ship decision.
It meaningfully slows the delivery of beneficial capabilities to the broader public, including users who would have benefited immediately and were never at meaningful risk.
Early access cohorts are frequently drawn from paying, technically sophisticated, or geographically concentrated users, so benefits accrue disproportionately to an already-advantaged group first.

StrategyScores.Description: Table: StrategyScores. A single numeric score (1-5) recording how a strategy performs against one shared criterion, with a short rationale. This is the join table that makes strategies comparable on the same stats across topics -- e.g. comparing an education strategy's Cost score directly against a regulation strategy's Cost score.

schema.name: ScoreId
schema.Description: Stored identifier for the score. Slug form, e.g. 'ai-proctored-open-exams__cost'.

schema.name: Name
schema.Description: Display alias for the score.

schema.name: Strategy
schema.Description: The strategy being scored.

schema.name: StrategyTitle
schema.Description: Title of the scored strategy.

schema.name: Criterion
schema.Description: The shared criterion being scored against.

schema.name: CriterionTitle
schema.Description: Title of the criterion.

schema.name: CriterionIcon
schema.Description: Icon of the criterion.

schema.name: Score
schema.Description: Score from 1 (very unfavorable on this criterion) to 5 (very favorable).

schema.name: Rationale
schema.Description: One-sentence rationale for why this strategy earned this score on this criterion.

data.Rationale: Requires licensed AI access, proctoring/logging software, and materially more teacher grading time per exam.
Schools with device fleets, bandwidth, and AI licensing budgets can run this well; resource-poor schools cannot administer it credibly.
Requires retraining teachers to write an entirely new question format, not just changing a policy line.
When well-authored, it tests the exact synthesis/judgment skill that matters in an AI-saturated world.
Full AI query logs give graders and auditors a rich, inspectable trail of what the student saw and did.
Students can still pre-script 'safe' responses, though logged transcripts make wholesale copying easier to catch.
Question formats and proctoring tools can be rolled back, but teacher retraining investment is partly sunk.
Licensing costs are modest compared to proctoring or infrastructure builds, and it reduces teacher grading hours.
Can narrow gaps with unlimited patient tutoring, but only if the school can afford the tool for everyone.
Slots into an existing draft-and-revise workflow most classrooms already use.
Works well for mechanical feedback but is weaker at judging originality and voice.
Comments and responses are visible and reviewable, but the model's rubric weighting is usually a black box.
Students can learn to superficially satisfy comment-resolution requirements without genuinely revising.
Dropping the tool and reverting to fully manual feedback is a low-friction, low-cost change.
Oral defenses and in-class writing require significantly more staff time per student at scale.
Disadvantages students with disabilities, testing anxiety, or English-language-learner status.
Requires redesigning assessment structure and often expanding grading staff.
A live oral defense is one of the hardest formats to fake and reliably surfaces real understanding.
Verifiable in the moment, but there's often no durable record unless sessions are recorded.
Live, unscripted follow-up questioning is about as resistant to AI-assisted gaming as an assessment format gets.
Policy can be reversed quickly, but staffing changes made to support it are stickier to unwind.
Building new curriculum, training teachers, and licensing practice tools is a substantial upfront investment.
Once built, the core skill needs minimal ongoing AI access, narrowing rather than widening resource gaps.
New curriculum development and standards alignment is a multi-year process, not a policy memo.
Teaching evaluation and verification skills addresses the actual underlying competency gap directly.
Student portfolios and prompt audits create a concrete, reviewable artifact trail.
The graded skill is catching errors, not producing polished output, so it's harder to outsource to AI itself.
Once curriculum, staffing, and standards alignment are institutionalized, unwinding them is a multi-year process too.
Mostly a policy and rubric change; requires an LLM access tool but little new infrastructure.
Outcomes depend heavily on prompting skill, which is unevenly distributed across students.
Can be piloted in a single classroom quickly since it mainly changes the assignment format.
Encourages genuine exploration but trades off structured-writing practice that essays build.
The full conversation transcript gives the teacher direct visibility into the student's reasoning process.
A student could still have someone else drive the conversation, though the transcript makes this more visible than a submitted essay.
Reverting to traditional essays is a simple policy change with no sunk infrastructure.
Labeling requirements are cheap to implement -- a UI string, a disclaimer line -- with no new technical infrastructure.
Low compliance cost means small and large companies face roughly the same burden.
Can be legislated and complied with in months, changing labeling practice rather than system architecture.
Disclosure alone does not address whether the underlying AI system is safe, accurate, or fair.
The disclosure itself is easy to verify, but the law does nothing to make the system's internal behavior auditable.
A bad actor can comply with the letter of the requirement while still deploying a manipulative system underneath it.
A labeling law can be amended or repealed with minimal entrenched infrastructure to unwind.
Licensing fees, audit costs, and compliance staff represent a major ongoing expense for covered organizations.
Compliance costs are largely fixed regardless of company size, falling disproportionately on smaller developers.
Standing up a licensing body and accrediting auditors is a multi-year regulatory build-out.
Independent, recurring audits are proven in other regulated industries to surface hidden harms.
Mandatory, independent, periodic review is close to the definition of an externally verifiable system.
Thresholds can be gamed, but the recurring audit cycle limits how long gaming can go undetected.
Once a licensing bureaucracy and accredited-auditor market exist, unwinding them is politically and operationally costly.
A well-understood infrastructure pattern that's cheap to implement relative to most safety interventions.
Treats accounts similarly at the individual level, but well-funded actors can provision multiple accounts.
Most platforms already have rate-limiting infrastructure; extending it is largely a configuration exercise.
Reliably contains runaway volume but does nothing to stop a low-volume, high-precision misuse case.
Throttle events are naturally logged as discrete, timestamped occurrences.
Sophisticated actors can distribute activity across accounts or stay just under the threshold.
A rate-limit threshold can be adjusted or removed with a configuration change in minutes.
Requires dedicated monitoring infrastructure and incident-response staffing at each stage.
Early-access cohorts tend to skew toward paying or technically sophisticated users.
Mechanics are well-established, but building genuinely meaningful monitoring gates takes real engineering investment.
Directly validated by precedent -- clinical trials, aviation certification -- as effective at catching low-probability, high-severity failures.
Stage gates exist, but advancement criteria are typically set unilaterally with no external visibility.
Hard for an outside actor to game since expansion is gated on the developer's own monitoring rather than a calendar date.
A stage can be paused or rolled back to a smaller cohort quickly since the mechanism is designed around gated advancement.
